sections.title: How is vegetative propagation in plants helpful in agriculture?
How does meiosis help create variations in sexual reproduction?
How does the process of pollination occur in flowers?

slides.title: One Parent Is Enough
slides.kicker: Copying life without a partner, ekdum simple!
bullets: Asexual reproduction needs only one parent and produces genetically identical individuals.
It is common in unicellular organisms like bacteria, amoeba and yeast.
Simple multicellular organisms like hydra and sponge also reproduce asexually.
Many plants use this mode too, growing new individuals from their existing parts.
slides.note: One parent, zero drama, exact copies.

slides.title: Plants From Plant Parts
slides.kicker: No seeds needed, kaise? Read on.
bullets: Potato and ginger have fleshy underground stems that sprout new plants without seeds.
Money plant and sugarcane stem cuttings grow into complete new plants.
Bryophyllum leaves sprout tiny plantlets which eventually grow into new plants.
All of these are examples of vegetative propagation from growing parts of a plant.
slides.note: Stems, cuttings, leaves, sab jagah new plants.

slides.title: Why Copies Look Alike
slides.kicker: The key point you must remember.
bullets: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent, never two.
Because there is one parent, the offspring are genetically identical individuals.
No mixing of genetic material happens, so no new combinations of characters appear.
This natural process is exactly what farmers and horticulturists later adapt for their use.
slides.note: One parent in, identical copies out.

slides.title: Growing Plants From Cuttings
slides.kicker: Gardeners do this every season, dekho.
bullets: Gardeners cut overgrown branches of a plant at the end of its growing season and prepare cuttings.
Collect shoot cuttings in the morning and remove leaves from the lower half of each cutting.
Insert cuttings up to about half their length in soil mixed with compost, at 45 to 60 degrees.
Water them regularly and observe the new growth appear.

items: Insert half length in compost soil at 45 to 60 degrees

slides.note: 45 to 60 degree angle, yaad rakhna!

slides.title: Grafting Joins Two Plants
slides.kicker: Two plants, one future, jodi No. 1.
bullets: Take a healthy rooted plant A, for example a wild rose variety.
Cut a healthy stem piece from plant B of another variety, like a yellow or pink rose plant.
Make a wound or slit on a twig of plant A and insert and fit the stem of plant B into it.
Protect the slit with a cotton cloth or wrapping film so pests stay out until the graft heals.

items: Cut stem piece from plant B
Fit B into a slit on A
Cover the wound till it heals

slides.note: Wild rose roots plus fancy rose stem equals high-yield plant.

slides.title: Propagation Feeds Farmers
slides.kicker: Science meets the kheti-badi.
bullets: Scientists and horticulturists adapted natural asexual reproduction into cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture.
These methods propagate plants efficiently and have greatly improved agricultural and horticultural practices.
Farmers can cultivate desirable crops on a large scale using these techniques.
Krishi Vigyan Kendras under ICAR teach farmers modern grafting skills and marketing strategies.
slides.note: KVK under ICAR, farmers ka skill upgrade centre.

slides.title: Two Parents, Shared Legacy
slides.kicker: Ab dono milke banate hain naya jeev.
bullets: Sexual reproduction involves two parents in the formation of a new individual.
Both parents contribute to the genetic material of the offspring.
This mixing of material from two individuals is what sets sexual reproduction apart from asexual.
Offspring therefore carry characters from both parents, not from a single parent alone.
slides.note: Two parents, shared genetic contribution.

slides.title: The Doubling Danger
slides.kicker: A biological problem hiding in plain sight.
bullets: Each parent passes genetic material to the offspring during sexual reproduction.
If each generation received the full set of chromosomes from both parents, the number would keep growing.
The chromosome number would double in every single generation, which cannot continue.
Nature solves this biological problem with a special type of cell division called meiosis.
slides.note: Doubling every generation? Meiosis says no.

slides.title: Meet Meiosis
slides.kicker: The special division that saves the day.
bullets: Meiosis is a special type of cell division that forms the cells used for reproduction.
It reduces the chromosome number of a parent cell so the total stays fixed across generations.
The cells it produces are called gametes, and they are used only for reproduction.
The next sections explore how meiosis also quietly creates variations among offspring.
slides.note: Meiosis forms gametes, the reproduction team.

slides.title: Chromosomes Carry Information
slides.kicker: Nucleus ke andar chhupi hui library.
bullets: Chromosomes are thread-like structures present in the nucleus of a cell.
They carry the genetic information of an organism.
Each species has a fixed number of chromosomes in its cells.
Humans have 23 pairs, one chromosome of each pair coming from each of two different parents.
slides.note: Humans: 23 pairs, 46 total.

slides.title: Meiosis Halves the Number
slides.kicker: Diploid se haploid, number half ho gaya.
bullets: In meiosis, the chromosome number of a diploid parent cell is reduced to half, making haploid cells.
The haploid cells are used only for reproduction and are called gametes.
In animals, male gametes are called sperm and female gametes are called eggs.
In plants, the pollen grain contains male gametes and the ovule contains the female gametes.
slides.note: Diploid to haploid, that is the meiosis magic.

slides.title: Shuffling Builds Variety
slides.kicker: Beads khelo, genetics samjho.
bullets: During meiosis, the chromosomes of each pair separate so every gamete gets one from each pair.
Each human gamete has 23 chromosomes, each carrying information for many characters.
In the bead activity, just three pairs of characters give eight possible combinations.
This random mixing makes children genetically different, which is the heart of variation.

items: Pick one bead from each pair

slides.note: 3 pairs give 8 combos. Imagine 23 pairs!

slides.title: Flowers Are Reproductive Organs
slides.kicker: Sundar bhi, smart bhi.
bullets: Flowering plants, called angiosperms, are the most diverse group of plants on Earth.
Flowers serve as the reproductive organs in angiosperms.
Non-flowering plants like pines also reproduce sexually, which you will study in the next chapter.
Leaves photosynthesise and roots absorb water, while flowers take charge of reproduction.
slides.note: Angiosperms, the most diverse plant group.

slides.title: Four Whorls of a Flower
slides.kicker: Sepal se pistil tak, poori team.
bullets: A complete flower has four parts: sepals, petals, stamens and pistil.
Sepals are the thin, flat green covering that protects the flower in the bud stage.
Petals are the coloured projections that enhance the beauty and attraction of the flower.
In some flowers both sepals and petals are fused, which you notice while dissecting buds.
slides.note: Four whorls: sepal, petal, stamen, pistil.

slides.title: Stamen and Pistil
slides.kicker: Male part meets female part.
bullets: The stamen is the male part of the flower, made of a filament and an anther.
The anther produces pollen grains, which contain the male gametes.
The pistil is the female part with three subparts: stigma, style and the swollen ovary at the base.
Cutting a longitudinal section of the ovary reveals the parts hidden inside.
slides.note: Anther equals pollen factory; stigma is the landing pad.

slides.title: What Is Pollination?
slides.kicker: Pollen ki safar, stigma tak.
bullets: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of a flower.
It is the first step towards the formation of fruits and seeds.
Without this transfer, the male gametes can never reach the female gametes.
Nature has provided plants with various strategies to make pollination happen.
slides.note: Pollination equals pollen reaching the stigma.

slides.title: Self Versus Cross
slides.kicker: Ghar ke andar ya padosi tak?
bullets: Self-pollination: pollen lands on the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant.
Cross-pollination: pollen moves from the anther of one plant to the stigma of another plant of the same type.
Both types end with pollen sitting on a stigma, ready for the next step.
Think ahead: what would happen to fruits and seeds if pollination never occurred?

left.title: Self-pollination
items: Or another flower on the same plant

right.title: Cross-pollination
items: Stigma of another plant of the same type

slides.note: Same plant is self, different plant is cross.

slides.title: Why Pollination Matters
slides.kicker: No pollination, no fruits, phir?
bullets: The transfer of pollen grains to the stigma is important for the formation of fruits and seeds.
Pollination cannot always happen on its own, so plants depend on outside help.
External agents called pollinators carry pollen from flower to flower.
If pollination does not occur, fruits and seeds fail to form, threatening the next generation.
slides.note: No pollination means no fruits and no seeds.

slides.title: Wind and Water Couriers
slides.kicker: Hawa aur paani bhi kamaal karte hain.
bullets: In wheat, maize and rice, pollen grains are light and small and produced in large numbers.
Wind-pollinated flowers have a long and feathery stigma to trap drifting pollen.
In aquatic plants like Vallisneria and Hydrilla, water currents carry pollen from one flower to another.
These strategies show how different plants match their pollen design to their carrier.
slides.note: Feathery stigma catches pollen like a net.

slides.title: Insect Couriers
slides.kicker: Bee ko bulao, pollination karao.
bullets: Sunflower, hibiscus and marigold are pollinated by insects such as bees and butterflies.
Their flowers are brightly coloured, produce nectar and give off fragrance to attract pollinators.
Their pollen grains are large, sticky or spiny, so they attach to the insect's body.
The stigma is also sticky, so it can receive the pollen carried by visiting insects.
slides.note: Sticky pollen, sticky stigma, perfect handshake.

slides.title: Birds as Pollinators
slides.kicker: Chidiya bhi madad karti hai.
bullets: Some flowers, like those of the coral tree and the hibiscus plant, are pollinated by birds.
Bird pollinators named in the book include the Indian white-eye and sunbirds.
Bird pollination is another strategy that raises the chances of reproductive success.
Every pollination strategy exists to help the plant form fruits and seeds successfully.
slides.note: Sunbirds sip and spread pollen on the way.

slides.title: Pollen Tube's Journey
slides.kicker: Stigma se ovule tak, tube express.
bullets: Once pollen reaches a compatible stigma, it produces a pollen tube.
The tube grows down through the style into the ovary.
The male gamete moves through this tube and arrives at the ovule.
There it fuses with the egg cell, and a remarkable new life begins.
slides.note: Pollen tube, gamete ka tunnel train.

slides.title: Zygote, Fruit and Seeds
slides.kicker: Fusion se fruit tak ka safar.
bullets: The fusion of gametes is called fertilisation, and it marks the beginning of a new life.
The fertilised egg is called a zygote, which later develops into an embryo.
The ovary surrounding the ovules enlarges and develops into a fruit.
The ovules develop into seeds inside the fruit.

items: Ovary to fruit, ovules to seeds

slides.note: Ovary becomes fruit, ovule becomes seed.

slides.title: Dispersal and Germination
slides.kicker: Naye jagah, nayi shuruaat.
bullets: Seed dispersal takes place by wind, by water and by animals.
When conditions like water, air and temperature are favourable, the seed germinates.
A germinated seed grows into a new plant, continuing the cycle.
Sexual reproduction creates variation, helping plant species survive and adapt to their environment.
slides.note: Madar and dandelion seeds ride the wind.

slides.title: Animals Reproduce Too
slides.kicker: Budding, spores, ya do parents?
bullets: Reproduction in animals takes place through asexual or sexual methods, or both.
Asexual methods like budding and spore formation were studied earlier in this chapter.
Animals such as frogs and most fish rely on sexual reproduction.
Where the fertilisation happens, outside or inside the body, decides their strategy.
slides.note: Animals: asexual, sexual, or dono.

slides.title: External Fertilisation
slides.kicker: Paani mein milte hain gametes.
bullets: In frogs and most fish, fertilisation occurs outside the body of the parents.
The female releases eggs into the water and the male releases sperm over the eggs.
This method of fertilisation is called external fertilisation.
Although a large number of eggs are laid, many are destroyed by water currents or eaten by other animals.
slides.note: Thousands of eggs, kyunki bahut loss hota hai.

slides.title: Internal Fertilisation
slides.kicker: Suraksha andar, survival upar.
bullets: In reptiles, birds and mammals, fertilisation takes place inside the body of the female.
This method is called internal fertilisation.
The fertilised egg or embryo is protected more when it develops inside the mother.
So the chances of survival of the young ones are generally higher with internal fertilisation.
slides.note: Inside the body, embryo ki extra security.

slides.title: The Survival Challenge
slides.kicker: Har animal ka bada sawaal.
bullets: Animals show a wide variety of methods of sexual reproduction.
All animals face one basic challenge: making sure male and female gametes meet.
The second part of the challenge: young ones must survive long enough to grow and reproduce.
The book compares four categories of animals in Table 11.4 to see different solutions.
slides.note: Gametes meet karo, young ones bachao.

slides.title: Many Eggs, Feeding Larva
slides.kicker: Kam yolk, zyada eggs, smart plan.
bullets: Fish, amphibians and insects produce several hundred to several thousand eggs at a time.
Each egg carries yolk with nutritive substances, but only enough to produce a larva.
The larva hatches and gets nutrition by eating organic wastes like rotten food and manures.
After enough nutrition, a transformation forms the adult body, as in butterflies and frogs.
slides.note: Larva is the feeding stage of development.

slides.title: Few Eggs, Full Nourishment
slides.kicker: Kam eggs, poora pyaar.
bullets: Reptiles and birds lay eggs, and each egg contains enough yolk to nourish the embryo until hatching.
The young one hatches fully formed from a well-stocked egg.
In mammals, the zygote grows and develops inside the female body instead.
Fewer young ones are produced, but each receives far more nourishment and protection.
slides.note: Yolk-rich eggs or mother's body, dono kaam karte hain.

They exchange pollen with each other

quiz.q: Meiosis changes a diploid parent cell into:
quiz.why: The chromosome number is reduced to half, and the haploid cells are gametes.

quiz.why: Random mixing during meiosis provides many combinations, making children genetically different.

quiz.why: A complete flower has sepals, petals, stamens and a pistil.

quiz.why: The anther produces pollen grains which contain the male gametes.

examples.title: Halving and restoring the human chromosome number
examples.problem: A human body cell has 23 pairs of chromosomes. Trace the chromosome number through meiosis and fertilisation, and explain why it stays fixed every generation.
steps: A diploid human body cell carries 46 chromosomes, arranged as 23 pairs, one chromosome of each pair from each of two parents.
During meiosis, the chromosomes of each pair separate, reducing the diploid number to haploid.
Each resulting human gamete, sperm or egg, therefore carries only 23 chromosomes.
At fertilisation, sperm and egg fuse, so the zygote again has 23 pairs, a total of 46 chromosomes.
examples.answer: Each gamete has 23 chromosomes and the zygote restores 46, so the human chromosome number stays fixed in every generation.

examples.title: Counting gamete combinations like Activity 11.4
examples.problem: In the bead activity, three bead pairs represent three contrasting characters, like hair colour, hair type and eye colour. How many combinations can one gamete carry, and what does this suggest for 23 pairs?
steps: Each gamete receives one bead, that is one chromosome, from each of the 3 pairs.
So the independent choices multiply: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations, exactly as the book confirms.
With 23 pairs of chromosomes, the same rule gives 2 multiplied by itself 23 times, written as 2^23.
2^23 works out to 8388608, and each of those gametes carries information for many characters.
examples.answer: 8 combinations with three bead pairs; with 23 pairs, 2^23, that is 8388608 possible gamete combinations, which is why children differ.

examples.title: Matching flowers to their pollination strategy
examples.problem: Classify the pollination strategy of wheat, Vallisneria, sunflower and coral tree using the flower features described in the chapter.
steps: Wheat has light and small pollen grains produced in large numbers and a long feathery stigma, so it is wind pollinated, like maize and rice.
Vallisneria and Hydrilla are aquatic plants whose pollen is carried by water currents, so they are water pollinated.
Sunflower, like hibiscus and marigold, is brightly coloured, produces nectar and fragrance, and has large sticky or spiny pollen, so insects like bees pollinate it.
The coral tree is pollinated by birds such as the Indian white-eye and sunbirds.
examples.answer: Wheat uses wind, Vallisneria uses water, sunflower uses insects, and the coral tree uses birds for pollination.

examples.title: From pollen grain to fruit in a china-rose
examples.problem: A pollen grain lands on the stigma of a china-rose (hibiscus or gudhal) flower. Describe the complete path from pollination to fruit and seed formation.
steps: The compatible pollen grain germinates and produces a pollen tube that grows down through the style into the ovary.
The male gamete moves through this tube and arrives at the ovule, where it fuses with the egg cell.
This fusion is fertilisation; the fertilised egg, called the zygote, later develops into an embryo.
Meanwhile the ovary surrounding the ovules enlarges and develops into a fruit, and the ovules develop into seeds inside it.
examples.answer: Pollen tube grows down the style, gametes fuse in the ovule, the zygote becomes an embryo, the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

flowchart.title: How reproduction flows in this chapter

steps.label: One parent copies itself
steps.detail: Asexual reproduction in bacteria, amoeba, yeast, hydra and many plants makes identical individuals.

steps.label: Plants propagate vegetatively
steps.detail: Farmers use cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture to grow desirable crops at scale.

steps.label: Two parents team up
steps.detail: Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from both parents in the offspring.

steps.label: Meiosis halves chromosomes
steps.detail: Diploid cells become haploid gametes, and shuffling creates many combinations.

steps.label: Pollination delivers pollen
steps.detail: Wind, water, insects or birds carry pollen to the stigma of a flower.

steps.label: Fertilisation forms zygote
steps.detail: A pollen tube carries the male gamete to the egg cell in the ovule, and they fuse.

steps.label: Fruit and seeds form
steps.detail: The ovary becomes the fruit, ovules become seeds, then dispersal and germination follow.

steps.label: Animals ensure survival
steps.detail: External or internal fertilisation, larval feeding stages or protected development keep young ones alive.
